DO NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk anyway).
DO NOT use `strings`, `objdump`, `nm`, `gdb`, or any binary/symbol inspection. Behavioral probing via command-line arguments ONLY.

The binary's driver program is exactly this:

  inflection::Inflector::initialize();
  std::vector<std::string> results;
  for (int i = 1; i < argc && i <= 5; i++) {
      std::string word = argv[i];
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::pluralize(word));
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::camelize(word));
      if (i % 2 == 0) results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::underscore(word));
  }
  for (const auto& r : results) std::cout << r << std::endl;
  if (argc > 1) {
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isPlural(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isSingular(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::demodulize("Module::" + std::string(argv[1])) << std::endl;
  }

So to observe a function on an arbitrary word W:
  - pluralize(W)  -> line 1 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - camelize(W)   -> line 2 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - underscore(W) -> `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable dummy "W"` prints: pluralize(dummy), camelize(dummy), pluralize(W), camelize(W), underscore(W), then isPlural/isSingular/demodulize of "dummy". So underscore(W) is line 5.
  - isPlural(W)   -> line 3 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"` (prints as 0/1 since it's a bool via operator<<)
  - isSingular(W) -> line 4 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - demodulize("Module::" + W) -> line 5 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`

Run MANY probes (hundreds). Use bash loops. Quote arguments properly. Capture stderr too (2>&1 separately from stdout when it matters) and capture exit codes.
Be systematic: form a hypothesis, then design inputs that DISCRIMINATE between competing hypotheses, then confirm.
Report the exact rule as precise pseudocode operating on BYTES (the C++ code uses std::string = bytes; the "C" locale means std::toupper/tolower only affect ASCII a-z/A-Z). Explicitly test non-ASCII UTF-8 input to confirm byte-level behavior.

Initial probing (line 2 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`) gave:

findings: Only the byte '_' (0x5F) is a word separator. Exhaustive scan of camelize("a" + b + "b") for every byte b in 0x21..0x7E plus 0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20,0x7F and all of 0x80..0xFF: the output equals the input verbatim for every b except 0x5F, which yields "aB".

Exhaustive scan of camelize("x_" + b + "y") for every byte b: only b in 'a'..'z' (0x61..0x7A) is changed, and it is changed to b-0x20. Digits ('a_1'->'a1'), symbols ('a_-b'->'a-b', 'a_.b'->'a.b', 'a_/b'->'a/b', 'a_:b'->'a:b'), space ('a_ b'->'a b'), tab ('a_\tb'->'a\tb'), already-uppercase ('a_B'->'aB'), 0x7F, and every byte 0x80..0xFF pass through byte-for-byte unchanged. This proves ASCII-only std::toupper ("C" locale) with no Latin-1/locale mapping.

The capitalize flag is cleared by ANY consumed byte, not only by a letter. Discriminating input: "a_\tb" -> "a\tb" (byte-loop model), NOT "a\tB" (which a 'skip until first letter' model would produce). Likewise "a_-b" -> "a-b" and "_ _a" -> " A".

Runs of underscores collapse: 'a___b'->'aB', 'a__b'->'aB', '__a__b__'->'AB'. Leading underscores capitalize the first surviving byte: '___a'->'A', '_hello'->'Hello', '_ABC'->'ABC', '_x_y_z_'->'XYZ'. Trailing underscores emit nothing: 'a___'->'a', 'a_b_'->'aB'. All-underscore input returns the empty string ('_', '__', '___', '____', and 20000 underscores all -> "").

camelize never lowercases anything. The first byte is emitted verbatim unless it was preceded by '_': 'Hello'->'Hello', 'HELLO'->'HELLO', 'Hello_World'->'HelloWorld', 'ABC_DEF'->'ABCDEF', 'ONE_two_THREE'->'ONETwoTHREE', 'aBc_dEf'->'aBcDEf', 'camelCase_test'->'camelCaseTest', 'Foo__Bar'->'FooBar', 'A_b'->'AB'.

No Rails-style special handling of '/' or '::'. 'active_record/errors' -> 'activeRecord/errors', 'a_b/c_d' -> 'aB/cD', 'a_b::c_d' -> 'aB::cD', 'Module::foo_bar' -> 'Module::fooBar'. '/' is NOT converted to '::' and ':' is not a separator.

Whitespace is never trimmed and never acts as a separator: '  a_b  ' -> '  aB  ', ' _a' -> ' A', 'a_ ' -> 'a '. Newlines pass through literally (camelize("a
b") == "a
b", camelize("_
a") == "
a" — the '
' consumes the capitalize flag and is emitted unchanged).

UTF-8 is handled as raw bytes with no multi-byte awareness: camelize('a_é') == 'a' 0xC3 0xA9 (the 0xC3 lead byte consumes the capitalize flag and is emitted unchanged); camelize('ünïcode_tëst') == 0xC3 0xBC 'n' 0xC3 0xAF 'code' 'T' 0xC3 0xAB 'st' (i.e. 'ünïcodeTëst') — the ASCII 't' after '_' is uppercased, no non-ASCII byte is ever altered.

camelize('') == '' and does not throw. (The program does abort with std::out_of_range on empty argv[1], but that comes from demodulize("Module::") after camelize's output has already been printed — stdout is "

0
1
", exit 134.)

No length limit or truncation: a 5999-byte input of 2000 '_'-joined 'ab' tokens produced exactly the expected 4000-byte 'ab' + 'Ab'x1999. 5000 underscores followed by 'x' -> 'X'. 20000 underscores -> ''.
Stateless / idempotent across calls: passing the same word multiple times in one invocation (a_b a_b c_d a_b e_f) yields identical results each time; results do not depend on argument position.

800 randomized differential tests (letters/underscores/digits/space/tab/'-'/'.'/'/'/':'/high bytes, plus fully random bytes 0x01..0xFF excluding 0x0A with 30% underscore bias, lengths 1..12) matched the byte-loop reference implementation with zero mismatches.

uncertainties: Behavior on an embedded NUL byte (0x00) inside the string is untestable through argv; the driver builds std::string from a C string so a NUL can never reach camelize via this harness. A std::string-based loop would presumably treat 0x00 as an ordinary non-'_' byte, but this is unverified.

The internal implementation (explicit byte loop vs. split-on-'_' + capitalize-each-token-after-the-first) cannot be distinguished: both models agree on every input probed, including empty tokens from consecutive/leading/trailing underscores. The pseudocode above is behaviorally exact either way.

Only the "C" locale was exercised (no locale env manipulation was attempted). If the binary were run under a locale where std::toupper maps bytes >= 0x80, output could in principle differ; under the observed default environment no byte outside 0x61..0x7A is ever modified.
